question: Do hyperparameter loss landscapes share stable structural and ranking patterns across models, datasets, train/test splits, and fidelity levels that could explain transfer and multi-fidelity HPO?

key_findings.claim: Across the studied classical, ensemble, and small-CNN models, discretized hyperparameter landscapes are usually smooth, locally clustered, highly neutral, and effectively close to unimodal.
key_findings.evidence: More than 1,500 landscapes from over 11 million evaluated configurations show high autocorrelation and loss assortativity. Most extra local optima have small attraction basins, and neutral moves become more prevalent near the best region, consistent with diminishing returns. NASBench landscapes retain smoothness/neutrality but have many more local optima, making the near-unimodal conclusion model-family dependent.

key_findings.claim: Training and test landscapes can look structurally similar while disagreeing precisely in the top configurations that HPO cares about.
key_findings.evidence: For most models, global train/test rank correlation has median above 0.7 and Shake-up below 0.15, and local-optimum counts are nearly identical. Yet top-10% set overlap is generally low. XGBoost is the stark case: median Spearman is 0.34, Shake-up 0.25, and top-set Jaccard-like gamma similarity 0.07; high learning rate, deep trees, and low subsampling interact to produce overfit configurations.

key_findings.claim: Low-fidelity landscapes are often useful rank proxies for full training, providing direct landscape-level support for early-stopping HPO, but long-tail failures remain.
key_findings.evidence: Using 10% training data or fewer epochs, most model/dataset pairs have median low/full-fidelity Spearman above 0.85, top-10% overlap above 60%, and mean rank movement below 10%. NASBench-201 obtains a reasonable ordering after 10 of 200 epochs. The distributions have long tails, so these aggregates do not license indiscriminate early stopping on every task.

key_findings.claim: Landscape transfer across datasets is meaningful within related task families but weaker in the elite region and can collapse under domain shift.
key_findings.evidence: For a fixed model, cross-dataset performance ranks have median Spearman above 0.65 and top-10% overlap around 40%, with recurring important hyperparameters/interactions. NASBench-201 transfers among CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-16-120, whereas NASBench-360 biomechanics and computational-physics tasks deviate substantially. Simple dataset meta-features correlate with some landscape similarities but are not a complete transfer criterion.

method.core_idea: Represent exhaustively sampled HPO grids as directed neighborhood graphs, characterize their topology with fitness-landscape metrics, and compare paired landscapes using configuration-rank agreement.
method.mechanism: Each configuration is a node; categorical and numerical grid-step distances define distance-one neighbors, with edges directed toward lower loss. Six measures cover smoothness, local loss clustering, neutrality, flattening near optima, local-optimum count, and basin size. HOPE graph embeddings followed by UMAP and interpolation provide 2D surfaces. Spearman rank correlation, Kaggle Shake-up, and top-gamma set overlap compare train/test, fidelity, and dataset pairs. Exhaustive grids cover DT, SVM, XGBoost, RF, LightGBM, CNN, and existing NAS benchmarks.
assumptions: A distance-one move on a hand-designed mixed grid is a meaningful and comparable local hyperparameter perturbation.
The selected ranges and resolutions contain the practically relevant landscape and do not distort modality.
Five-fold evaluation adequately controls sampling noise so configuration rankings can be compared as fixed landscapes.
Rank-based similarity captures HPO transfer value better than raw-loss similarity.
Aggregating distributions across datasets and models is informative despite heterogeneous metrics and task sizes.

techniques.role: Encodes local hyperparameter moves and their downhill loss direction.
Measures autocorrelation, assortativity, neutrality, optimum flattening, modality, and basin size.
Embeds high-order directed-graph proximity and projects it for qualitative visualization.
Uses global correlation, expected rank movement, and elite-set overlap for paired landscapes.
Identifies recurring hyperparameter and interaction contributions across datasets.
Makes topology observable rather than inferring it from sparse optimizer trajectories.

evaluations.setting: DT, SVM, XGBoost, RF, LightGBM, and CNN grids over 63 tabular/image datasets
evaluations.metric: Six landscape features and three pairwise rank-similarity measures
evaluations.result: Most landscapes are smooth, clustered, neutral, and nearly unimodal, with important exceptions in elite-region agreement and XGBoost generalization.
evaluations.baseline: Prior isolated AutoML landscape studies with fewer model-task combinations

evaluations.metric: Spearman, Shake-up, and top-10% set similarity
evaluations.result: Median correlations exceed 0.85, elite overlap exceeds 60%, and rank movement is under 10% for most cases, with long-tail outliers.

evaluations.metric: Topology features, rank similarity, elite overlap, and hyperparameter-conditioned generalization gaps
evaluations.result: Global/local topology is often stable, but elite overlap is low and XGBoost exhibits severe interacting overfit modes.
evaluations.baseline: Assumption that training rank is an adequate model-selection proxy

evaluations.metric: Modality, fidelity rank transfer, and cross-dataset similarity
evaluations.result: NAS is more multimodal; early ranks and related vision tasks transfer, while distant scientific tasks substantially reshape the landscape.

limitations: The model set excludes Transformers, GANs, large language models, and other expensive modern systems; the paper explicitly avoids universal claims.
Discrete, manually bounded grids can miss optima and create or erase local structure between sampled values.
Neighborhood geometry weights every categorical flip and numerical grid step equally, although their semantic and scale effects differ.
Neutrality depends on the chosen 0.1% tolerance, hyperparameter selection, domain, and grid resolution; there is no accepted standard.
HOPE, UMAP, and interpolation can make visually smooth surfaces that are not unique or metrically faithful representations of the original graph.
Exhaustive construction costs thousands of accelerator/CPU hours and cannot be used directly as an online HPO diagnostic at large scale.
Median similarities hide precisely documented long-tail failures and top-region disagreement, so aggregate evidence does not validate every transfer or early-stopping rule.
The study analyzes landscapes but does not run controlled optimizer comparisons to show that each measured property causally predicts HPO regret.
failure_modes: A coarse grid labels a landscape unimodal while a narrow, high-performing basin lies between points.
Training stochasticity changes configuration ranks enough that a single averaged graph is misleading.
Low-fidelity rank correlation is high globally but prunes the eventual optimum because elite-set agreement is poor.
Warm-start transfer fails after dataset/domain shift despite similar coarse landscape metrics.
A high-neutrality plateau deprives local search of direction and causes excessive evaluations near the optimum.
The 2D embedding visually suggests proximity between nodes that are not nearby in the original search graph.
An HPO method exploits smoothness in the enumerated grid but behaves differently in the continuous or conditional search space.
reusable_insights: Compare landscapes at both global rank and elite-set levels; high correlation does not guarantee good model selection.
Audit low-fidelity proxies for false-negative pruning, not merely median rank correlation.
Make neighborhood and neutrality definitions explicit because topology is representation-dependent.
Use landscape metrics to design tighter search spaces, then validate the change with optimizer regret.
Treat task-family similarity and domain shift as first-class variables in hyperparameter transfer.
Separate qualitative embedded surfaces from graph-native quantitative evidence.
open_questions: Can sparse sampling or surrogate models recover graph topology and elite basins without exhaustive grids?
Which landscape features predict the relative performance of Bayesian, evolutionary, bandit, and local-search HPO?
How stable are modality and neutrality across random seeds and finer/continuous search spaces?
Do large-model hyperparameter landscapes retain smoothness, or do scaling instabilities create qualitatively new topology?
Can dataset meta-features predict when low-fidelity or cross-task transfer will fail in the elite region?
How should conditional, hierarchical, and dynamically changing hyperparameters be represented geometrically?
Can an online optimizer update a calibrated uncertainty distribution over landscape structure?

competitive_landscape.title: AutoML Loss Landscapes
competitive_landscape.difference: Pushak and Hoos test AutoML landscapes for departures from unimodality/convexity and find weak hyperparameter interactions across a smaller scenario set. The reviewed study scales the census, emphasizes pairwise structural similarity, and adds fidelity, train/test, and cross-dataset comparisons.

competitive_landscape.title: HPO X ELA: Investigating Hyperparameter Optimization Landscapes by Means of Exploratory Landscape Analysis
competitive_landscape.difference: Schneider et al. connect ELA features for 30 XGBoost HPO problems to optimizer performance and comparable BBOB instances. The reviewed work covers more models/tasks and landscape similarity, but does less direct validation of feature-to-optimizer predictions.

competitive_landscape.title: AutoRL Hyperparameter Landscapes
competitive_landscape.difference: Mohan et al. show DQN, PPO, and SAC landscapes can change strongly over training time, motivating dynamic hyperparameters. This cautions against treating the reviewed supervised landscapes as stationary and supplies the AutoRL extension proposed in its conclusion.

competitive_landscape.title: ARLBench: Flexible and Efficient Benchmarking for Hyperparameter Optimization in Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: ARLBench selects a representative subset from large RL hyperparameter-landscape data to enable cheap HPO comparisons. It operationalizes the reviewed paper's call for reusable landscape assets while focusing on optimizer benchmarking and compute-efficient coverage rather than exhaustive topology.

novelty_assessment: The large paired-landscape census and simultaneous use of global ranks, rank movement, and elite overlap materially extend earlier AutoML landscape work. The most useful insight is not simply that landscapes are benign, which prior studies reported, but that coarse topology may transfer while elite configurations do not. Visualization is less evidential than the graph metrics, and causal claims about optimizer behavior remain to be tested. The contribution is a strong exploratory dataset/framework rather than a new HPO algorithm.
reviewer_notes: Read all 31 extracted pages, including metric definitions, grid/task details, primary results, visualization validation, NAS appendices, dataset meta-feature analysis, and stated limitations. Reported medians are retained with their long-tail and domain-shift qualifications. Four primary publisher/arXiv related works were checked on 2026-08-23.
